clue.text: Chronicler of pilgrims' progress

parts.note: the pilgrims are the company riding to Canterbury, and the poet who told their tales chronicled their journey; the phrase also nods at Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress

explanation.surface: Someone who wrote up a pilgrims' journey, perhaps Bunyan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pilgrims' progress' points to Bunyan, but the pilgrims here are those of The Canterbury Tales, whose author recorded their ride.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canterbury Tales record a band of pilgrims travelling to Canterbury, so its poet chronicled their journey.

clue.text: Constructor (from Thrace) of Alexander's Bridge

indicators.note: the writer is made out of the letters of Thrace, so 'from' signals that this word is rearranged into a name

explanation.surface: An ancient builder from Thrace who put up a bridge for Alexander the Great.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander's Bridge is Willa Cather's first novel, so its 'constructor' is its author, whose surname is an anagram of THRACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Willa Cather wrote the 1912 novel Alexander's Bridge, so she built it as an author.

clue.text: Prince James placed in valuable vessel

definitions.text: Prince James placed in valuable vessel

parts.words: Prince James placed in valuable vessel
parts.note: the prince is one Henry James created and put into his novel The Golden Bowl, the 'valuable vessel'

explanation.surface: A royal prince called James is stowed aboard a costly ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince James' reads as a royal; it is the prince of Henry James, the Italian hero of The Golden Bowl, and the 'vessel' is that bowl, not a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Amerigo is the Italian nobleman at the centre of Henry James's novel The Golden Bowl.

clue.text: Such writers produced Mrs Leicester's School, while not preserving Silence of the Lambs

definitions.text: Such writers produced Mrs Leicester's School, while not preserving Silence of the Lambs

parts.words: Such writers produced Mrs Leicester's School, while not preserving Silence of the Lambs
parts.note: Mrs Leicester's School was written jointly by Charles and Mary Lamb, so the Lambs were writing partners who did not keep silent

explanation.surface: Writers of a children's book are said to have broken the hush around the film The Silence of the Lambs.
explanation.walkthrough: The Silence of the Lambs suggests Thomas Harris; the Lambs are Charles and Mary Lamb, who shared the writing of Mrs Leicester's School and so broke their silence together.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles and Mary Lamb wrote Mrs Leicester's School together, making them joint writers of one book.

clue.text: "A glorious place, a glorious age, I tell you! A very Neon ——' " (Tom Wolfe, The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test)

definitions.text: "A glorious place, a glorious age, I tell you! A very Neon ——' " (Tom Wolfe, The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test)

parts.words: "A glorious place, a glorious age, I tell you! A very Neon ——' " (Tom Wolfe, The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: Wolfe's line calls the scene a glorious age of rebirth lit in neon

explanation.surface: A line from Tom Wolfe's account of Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A completion clue: the blank is the word for a cultural rebirth, the 'glorious age' of the line, here a neon one.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebirth of arts and learning is a glorious age, which is what the quoted speaker claims for his own neon-lit times.

clue.text: Reputed composer of overture to The Beggar's Opera shows vigour at American church

definitions.text: Reputed composer of overture to The Beggar's Opera

parts.note: pep means vigour or energy

explanation.surface: The man credited with the overture to Gay's ballad opera is energetic at an American church.
explanation.walkthrough: Johann Christoph Pepusch is credited with the overture and arrangements for The Beggar's Opera; 'reputed' allows for doubts over his share.
explanation.definitionFit: The German-born composer Johann Christoph Pepusch is credited with arranging the music for Gay's 1728 ballad opera.

clue.text: What the guests of Benson and Gissing do

definitions.text: What the guests of Benson and Gissing do

parts.words: What the guests of Benson and Gissing do
parts.note: E. F. Benson wrote ... Guests and George Gissing The ... Guest, so these guests hand over money

explanation.surface: A question about how visitors in two novelists' books behave.
explanation.walkthrough: The guests are those of two titles, Benson's Paying Guests and Gissing's The Paying Guest.
explanation.definitionFit: A paying guest settles a bill for board and lodging, which the guests in both titles do.

clue.text: Browning's was due his

parts.note: Browning's Pied ... of Hamelin rid the town of rats and was owed his fee, as in the saying about paying the musician his due

explanation.surface: Something of the poet Browning's was owed what was coming to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'pay the piper his due' meets Browning's poem, where Hamelin refuses the rat-catcher his promised fee.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's The Pied Piper of Hamelin features a musician who rids a town of rats and is cheated of his reward.

clue.text: They have a treble chance of hitting the high spots

definitions.text: They have a treble chance of hitting the high spots

parts.words: They have a treble chance of hitting the high spots
parts.note: the treble chance was a football pools bet, but here treble means the highest singing voice, whose owners reach the top notes

explanation.surface: Gamblers on the football pools hope to land a big win.
explanation.walkthrough: The treble chance was a popular British football pools bet; here 'treble' is the top vocal line and the 'high spots' are high notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Singers with the highest voice range, the Italian plural of the term, take treble parts and reach the top notes.

clue.text: Heart of de Vries and Tynan's Quaker

definitions.text: Heart of de Vries and Tynan's Quaker

parts.words: Heart of de Vries and Tynan's Quaker
parts.note: Peter De Vries wrote The ___ Heart and Katharine Tynan The ___ Quaker, and one adjective fills both titles

explanation.surface: The centre of a Dutch name and a Quaker known to a critic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of' suggests taking middle letters, but Heart and Quaker are the last words of two titles: De Vries's The Handsome Heart and Katharine Tynan's The Handsome Quaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The same good-looking adjective completes De Vries's novel The ___ Heart and Tynan's The ___ Quaker.

clue.text: Friend of Dr Livesey, said to be one of Shelley

indicators.note: the squire's name is spoken the same as the name of a member of Shelley's circle, so 'said to be' signals a sound-alike

parts.note: Edward John Trelawny was one of Shelley's circle of friends and arranged his cremation

explanation.surface: A companion of the doctor is supposedly one of the poet Shelley's set.
explanation.walkthrough: Squire Trelawney sails with Dr Livesey in Treasure Island; Shelley's friend Edward Trelawny spelt his name without the E but said it the same.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's Treasure Island the squire who funds the voyage is a close companion of Dr Livesey.

clue.text: Short son of the Hammer

parts.note: Charles Martel was called 'the Hammer', and his son the Frankish king was known as 'the Short'

explanation.surface: A small boy whose father is called the Hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' is not about height in the surface sense but the king's epithet; 'the Hammer' is Charles Martel, his father.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepin the Short, King of the Franks and father of Charlemagne, was the son of Charles Martel.

clue.text: Evans, novelist to lie about

indicators.note: the words to lie are moved about, so 'about' signals that their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Evans is a novelist prepared to tell lies.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot; 'about' shuffles TO LIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Ann Evans published Middlemarch and her other books under the pen name George Eliot.

clue.text: Old academicians never die

parts.note: members of the Académie française are nicknamed les Immortels, and those who never die are deathless beings

explanation.surface: A saying in the style of 'old soldiers never die', about elderly scholars.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'Old soldiers never die'; the forty members of the Académie française are nicknamed 'les Immortels'.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Académie française bear the nickname les Immortels, and beings who cannot die are deathless.

clue.text: She created a draught, opening Arthur's eyes

definitions.text: She created a draught, opening Arthur's eyes

parts.words: She created a draught, opening Arthur's eyes
parts.note: the enchantress of Arthurian legend brewed potions and schemed against King Arthur, revealing betrayals to him

explanation.surface: A woman made a breeze by opening something, waking Arthur up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draught' suggests a breeze from an opened window; it is a magic potion brewed by Arthur's enchantress half-sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Morgan le Fay is the sorceress half-sister of King Arthur, a maker of spells and potions in Malory.

clue.text: Its founder spoke thus, Nietzsche thought

definitions.text: Its founder spoke thus, Nietzsche thought

parts.words: Its founder spoke thus, Nietzsche thought
parts.note: Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra puts words into the mouth of the Persian prophet who founded this faith

explanation.surface: Nietzsche believed that the founder of something talked in this way.
explanation.walkthrough: Zarathustra is the Persian name of the prophet Zoroaster; Nietzsche's book imagines him speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Persian religion was founded by the prophet Zarathustra, the speaker in Nietzsche's book.

clue.text: 8 god in a changed Cyrenaican city

parts.note: 8 is the word handsome, and the handsome god is Apollo, ideal of male beauty

indicators.note: the words in and a are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A good-looking god in an altered city of ancient Libya.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 refers to the answer at 8-down, the word for good-looking; 'changed' rearranges IN A into NIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollonia was the port of Cyrene in ancient Cyrenaica, on the coast of modern Libya.

clue.text: Traces: those of love revealed by Shirley Ann Grau and Dan Jacobson

definitions.meaning: traces are signs or proof that something has happened

definitions.text: those of love revealed by Shirley Ann Grau and Dan Jacobson
definitions.meaning: both Shirley Ann Grau and Dan Jacobson wrote a novel titled The ___ of Love

explanation.surface: Marks of affection uncovered by two novelists.
explanation.definitionFit: Traces are proof that something happened, and both novelists published a book called The ___ of Love.

clue.text: Exceptionally 8 girl meets exceptionally 8 boy in Shakespearean tragedy

definitions.text: Exceptionally 8 girl meets exceptionally 8 boy in Shakespearean tragedy

parts.words: Exceptionally 8 girl meets exceptionally 8 boy in Shakespearean tragedy
parts.note: 8 is the word handsome: the girl is the goddess of beauty and the boy the beautiful youth she loves, in Shakespeare's narrative poem

explanation.surface: A good-looking girl and boy meet in one of Shakespeare's tragedies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exceptionally' suggests an anagram, but there is none: the goddess of beauty and the youth she loves are the extremely handsome pair, and the 'tragedy' is Shakespeare's narrative poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's 1593 poem tells how the goddess of love courts a beautiful youth who dies hunting a boar.

clue.text: Distinctions for French writers

parts.note: a word borrowed from French for fine shades of difference, which French writers prize

explanation.surface: Honours awarded to authors in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distinctions' suggests prizes; it means subtle differences of meaning, a word French writers would use in their own language.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtle shades of meaning are fine distinctions, and the word is French in origin.

clue.text: Progressing where Poirot solved murder

definitions.meaning: Poirot solved Murder on the Orient Express aboard a railway carriage

explanation.surface: A detective's case moving on to its solution.
explanation.definitionFit: Something under way is in progress, and Poirot solved Murder on the Orient Express aboard a locomotive-hauled express.

clue.text: Such actors do them badly

indicators.note: the words do them are done badly, put out of order, so 'badly' signals a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A remark that certain actors perform certain parts poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges DO THEM; the actors are followers of Stanislavski's system.
explanation.definitionFit: Method actors follow Stanislavski's system of living inside a role.

clue.text: Watkins work of passing interest

parts.note: Vernon Watkins wrote a poem and collection called The ___ ___, and that bell is tolled for a passing, a death

explanation.surface: A piece by Watkins that holds only fleeting appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of passing interest' sounds like faint praise; 'passing' means dying, and Vernon Watkins, a Welsh poet, wrote The Death Bell.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell tolled at someone's passing marks a death, and Vernon Watkins titled a poem and book after it.

clue.text: "The keen —, fellest of the fell" (James Thomson, Summer)

definitions.text: "The keen —, fellest of the fell" (James Thomson, Summer)

parts.words: "The keen —, fellest of the fell" (James Thomson, Summer)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: Thomson lists savage African beasts in Summer from The Seasons, and this one is the cruellest

explanation.surface: A line from James Thomson's poem Summer with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A completion clue: in Summer, from The Seasons, Thomson names a scavenging beast as the fiercest of the fierce.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomson's catalogue of wild animals in Summer names this African scavenger as the most savage of beasts.

clue.text: Werther loved her, as did Goethe himself, Mann recalled

definitions.text: Werther loved her, as did Goethe himself, Mann recalled

parts.words: Werther loved her, as did Goethe himself, Mann recalled
parts.note: Werther adores ... in Goethe's novel, modelled on ... Buff whom Goethe loved; Thomas Mann recalled her in a novel set in Weimar

explanation.surface: Goethe's hero and Goethe both loved a woman, a man remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mann' looks like 'man' but is Thomas Mann, whose novel Lotte in Weimar has the elderly Charlotte Buff visit Goethe.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte, the beloved of Werther, was based on Charlotte Buff, the heroine of Thomas Mann's Lotte in Weimar.

clue.text: Alcove in scenic Heart of Midlothian

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, so 'in' signals a run hidden across them

explanation.surface: A recess in a picturesque spot in the old Edinburgh district made famous by Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: The Heart of Midlothian is Scott's novel and an Edinburgh landmark; the alcove is hidden across 'sceNIC HEart'.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a shallow recess in a wall, the same thing as an alcove.

clue.text: Composer composes off a bench

indicators.note: the words off a bench are composed, put together in a new order

explanation.surface: A composer writes music while sitting on a bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composes' rearranges OFF A BENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Offenbach was the German-French composer of operettas and The Tales of Hoffmann.

clue.text: Poem starting off decently enough

indicators.note: the starts of the three words that follow are taken, one letter from each

explanation.surface: A poem that begins in a respectable enough way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' takes the first letter of each of 'off decently enough'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ode is a lyric poem addressed to a subject.

clue.text: Hartleyan shrimp

parts.note: in L. P. Hartley's novel The Shrimp and the Anemone, the shrimp is the timid boy who is the hero

explanation.surface: A small sea creature in a Hartley novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In L. P. Hartley's The Shrimp and the Anemone, the boy Eustace is the shrimp and his sister Hilda the anemone.
explanation.definitionFit: Eustace is the timid boy hero of Hartley's trilogy, compared to a shrimp in its first title.

clue.text: "The child ——' to be out of doors" (The Old Curiosity Shop)

definitions.text: "The child ——' to be out of doors" (The Old Curiosity Shop)

parts.words: "The child ——' to be out of doors" (The Old Curiosity Shop)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: in Dickens's novel Little Nell longs to escape outside

explanation.surface: A line from Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop with a verb missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A completion clue: the child is Little Nell, who longed to be outside.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means longed or pined, describing Little Nell's wish to be outdoors.
